messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Aleksander Novak is a 32-year-old single combat pilot of Polish-American descent who presented for psychological evaluation following a sexual assault perpetrated by a fellow officer — a man he had considered one of his closest friends and most trusted colleagues. The assault occurred approximately fourteen months ago during an off-base gathering, after a period of drinking. Aleksander had been alone with his assailant in a private room when the attack took place. The betrayal was not merely physical; it was architectural. The person who violated him was someone with whom he had shared cockpits, briefings, and the particular intimacy that forms between men who trust each other with their lives at altitude. That foundation — his faith in the judgment of people around him, in the coherence of a professional world he had devoted himself to — collapsed in a single night, and has not been rebuilt since.

In the weeks that followed, Aleksander found himself unable to sleep without waking in a cold sweat, heart hammering, the residue of nightmares clinging to him as he lay rigid in the dark. Those moments of waking became their own ordeal: disoriented, breathing hard, he would lie still and listen — genuinely listen — for sounds of someone entering his home. The creak of the building settling, a door in the corridor, a car outside, all of it registered as potential threat. He began sleeping with the lights on. He checked the locks multiple times each night. Even in the middle of his own apartment, a place that should have offered safety, he felt perpetually on guard, his nervous system refusing to accept the evidence of the room around him. Any ordinary sound — a colleague dropping a clipboard in the ready room, the hydraulic hiss of a hangar door — could send a jolt of alarm through him that left him shaking and embarrassed in equal measure.

What made the hypervigilance particularly consuming was that it fed directly on his appraisals of himself and others. He had come to believe, with a certainty that felt irrefutable, that he had been betrayed by someone he trusted — and that this betrayal revealed something true about the world and about his own naivety. He had lost faith not only in people but in the structured meritocracy of military life that he had once found meaningful. These convictions — that trust was a liability, that people were opaque and dangerous — meant that any situation he could not fully predict felt loaded with threat. Unpredictable situations, once a manageable feature of his profession, now activated the same alarm state as a direct danger signal. His appraisals of the world as fundamentally unsafe amplified his vigilance, making every ambiguous moment feel like the precursor to something terrible.

The loop was self-reinforcing in ways he could not easily articulate but clearly felt. When his threat monitoring was high — when he was already scanning the room, already braced — he became more likely to read ordinary behaviour as suspicious. A colleague lingering near his locker, a stranger making eye contact in the corridor: these registered as people acting suspiciously, which in turn spiked his arousal and confirmed, in his mind, that his wariness was justified. And that confirmation deepened his conviction that he was surrounded by potential betrayal, which kept the vigilance running. His body's responses — the startle, the sleeplessness, the inability to relax even at home — he interpreted not as symptoms of trauma but as evidence of personal failure. He was certain that he was a lousy coper, that other men in his position would have processed this and moved on, and this belief in his own inadequacy sat alongside his distrust of others and his lost faith, each reinforcing the other in a circuit he could not break by willpower alone.

Over months, the occupational consequences accumulated. His performance reviews remained technically adequate, but his commanding officer had noted his withdrawal, his shortened fuse in briefings, his refusal of social invitations. He had stopped eating in the mess hall when it was crowded. What finally brought him to seek help was a near-incident during a training exercise — a moment of delayed response that he knew, privately, had nothing to do with the aircraft. He came to his first session hoping, above all, that someone could tell him whether the person he was before that night still existed somewhere beneath all of this.
